The Complete Cold Brew Coffee Guide

Cold brew coffee is made by steeping coarsely ground beans in cold water for many hours instead of forcing hot water through them. The slow extraction pulls out the sweet, chocolatey compounds while leaving most of the bitter acids behind, which is why a good batch tastes smooth without any sugar. This guide walks through the ratio, the steep time, the equipment, and how to serve the final concentrate properly.

What ratio should I use?

The classic starting point is a 1:8 ratio of coffee to water by weight. For a stronger concentrate many roasters recommend 200g of coffee to 1.6 liters of water, which you can dilute later. Weigh the beans instead of scooping them, because volume measurements drift wildly between roasts.

StyleRatio
Ready to drink1:8
Concentrate1:5

How long should cold brew steep?

Steep for 12 hours at room temperature or up to 24 hours in the refrigerator. Longer steeps extract more body but can turn woody past that window. Taste a spoonful at the 12 hours mark and decide whether it needs more time.

A note on grind size

Grind coarse, like breadcrumbs. A fine grind over-extracts during the long steep and clogs every filter you own, leaving silt at the bottom of the glass.

Equipment you will need

  • A large jar or dedicated brewer
  • A coarse burr grinder for even grounds
  • A fine mesh filter or cheesecloth

Serving and dilution ideas

  1. Cut concentrate with equal parts water over ice
  2. Add a splash of oat milk for a softer cup
  3. Freeze concentrate into cubes for iced lattes
